question:
A class studies a linear model of the form $y=mx+c$, where $m$ and $c$ are unknown constants. Two observations from the model are represented by the points $(1,4)$ and $(3,10)$. The students use these observations to form two equations in $m$ and $c$, solve them by the inverse-matrix method, and then use the resulting model to predict another output value.

(a) Form the system of equations in $m$ and $c$ and express it as $AX=B$.

(b) Calculate $|A|$ and determine whether the model is uniquely defined.

(c) Find $A^{-1}$ and hence determine $m$ and $c$.

(d) Use the model to calculate $y$ when $x=5$ and verify both observations.
explanation:
(a)
Since $y=mx+c$, the point $(1,4)$ gives
$$m+c=4$$
The point $(3,10)$ gives
$$3m+c=10$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}m\\c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\10\end{bmatrix}$$

(b)
$$|A|=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1\\3 & 1\end{vmatrix}=1-3=-2$$
Since $|A|\neq0$, the coefficient matrix is invertible and the linear model is uniquely defined.

(c)
$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\-3 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1\\3 & -1\end{bmatrix}$$
Thus,
$$\begin{bmatrix}m\\c\end{bmatrix}=A^{-1}B$$
$$=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1\\3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\10\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}6\\2\end{bmatrix}$$
Therefore,
$$m=3,\quad c=1$$
The model is $y=3x+1$.

(d)
When $x=5$,
$$y=3(5)+1=16$$
Verification of the observations:
$$x=1\Rightarrow y=3(1)+1=4$$
$$x=3\Rightarrow y=3(3)+1=10$$
Hence, both observations are satisfied and the predicted value is $16$.

options.A:
(a) $m+c=4,\ 3m+c=10$
(b) $|A|=2$, so the model is unique
(c) $m=2,\ c=2$
(d) $y(5)=12$
options.B:
(a) $m+c=4,\ 3m+c=10$
(b) $|A|=-2$
(c) $m=3,\ c=1$
(d) $y(5)=15$, while both observations are satisfied
options.C:
(a) $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\3&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}m\\c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\10\end{bmatrix}$
(b) $|A|=-2$, so the model is uniquely defined
(c) $A^{-1}=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\3&-1\end{bmatrix}$ and $(m,c)=(3,1)$
(d) $y(5)=16$, and both observations are verified
